sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: Despite the effective roll‐out of COVID‐19 vaccines, immunocompromised patients have a higher risk of morbidity and mortality following SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. Allogeneic adoptive T‐cell immunotherapy is now established as an effective approach to treat viral diseases in immunocompromised patients. The objective of this study was to assess the safety of allogeneic virus‐specific T‐cell therapy in patients with COVID‐19.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using a repository of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T cells generated from healthy exposed volunteers, we conducted an open‐label phase I trial to assess the feasibility and safety of allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T cells in immune‐compromised cancer patients with COVID‐19.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Six participants at risk of severe COVID‐19 were enrolled and received SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy within 4 days of recruitment. The first five participants who received two infusions of allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy experienced no adverse events following treatment. Four of the six participants showed improvement in viral load following treatment and were alive at 12‐week follow‐up. One participant died 6 days after their second infusion, because of established pulmonary parenchymal damage following prolonged COVID infection. Another, who had underlying lupus nephritis, developed cytokine release syndrome and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage following a single infusion and was withdrawn from the study. They subsequently recovered from this serious adverse event.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy provides a platform to rapidly administer T cells to high‐risk COVID‐19 patients. It was associated with a reduced viral load and increased SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell responses in the majority of treated patients.
Keywords: COVID‐19, immunocompromised, SARS‐CoV‐2, VST therapy

abstract.p: In this study, we conducted an open‐label phase I trial to assess the feasibility and safety of allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2 specific T cells in immune‐compromised cancer patients with COVID‐19. Our observations in this study demonstrate that SARS‐CoV‐2 specific T‐cell therapy was well tolerated in the majority of patients and was co‐incident with improvement in clinical symptoms. However, we also observed that one patient with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus developed a severe adverse event following T‐cell therapy, highlighting that patients with an underlying autoimmune disorder may be at an increased risk of therapy associated complications.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2) infection is highly disruptive to cancer care, with immunocompromised individuals representing a group vulnerable to life‐threatening infectious complications and subject to delayed delivery of critical cancer therapies because of persistent active infection. The development of vaccines against SARS‐CoV‐2 was rapid, but studies have demonstrated that patients with haematological malignancies demonstrate reduced immunogenicity in response to COVID‐19 vaccines 1 , 2 and are at increased risk for persistent SARS‐CoV‐2 positivity. 3

T‐cell immunotherapy provides a targeted antigen‐specific treatment option for patients with potentially life‐threatening infectious complications. 4 , 5 , 6 Initial anti‐viral T‐cell immunotherapies were pioneered through the application of donor‐matched haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or, where possible, the derivation of virus‐specific T‐cell (VST) therapy from autologous (self‐derived) peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC). More recent approaches utilise cryopreserved T‐cell repositories, where VST with defined viral specificity is generated from allogeneic healthy donors and can be selected for immediate therapeutic intervention against the relevant pathogen. 7 , 8 This approach enables the rapid administration of antigen‐specific VST within days of diagnosis, which reduces the 2‐ to 4‐week therapeutic turnaround typically required to generate an autologous or donor‐derived therapy. In this study, we demonstrate the therapeutic application of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T cells to treat patients with haematological malignancies who failed to control SARS‐CoV‐2 viral load following standard anti‐viral interventions, or who were at high risk of severe COVID‐19.

sec.title: T‐cell therapy manufacturing
sec.p: To generate a bank of allogeneic VST for adoptive immunotherapy against SARS‐CoV‐2, we recruited six healthy volunteers whom we had previously screened for SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell responses (Supplementary table 1). These individuals were selected based on their HLA type. Allogeneic ‘off‐the‐shelf’ SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapies were generated from a single blood collection (350–400 mL) using a custom pool of peptide epitopes restricted through HLA class I and class II alleles, designed to stimulate SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Supplementary tables 2 and 3). The median CD3+ T‐cell percentage in the T‐cell products was 95% (range 87.3–99.7%) (Supplementary table 4). In contrast with typical VST products generated to treat herpesvirus‐associated diseases, the SARS‐CoV‐2 VST products contained predominantly CD4+ T cells. A median of 75.7% (range 13.5–91.2%) of CD3+ T cells within each product batch were CD4+, while a median of 19.9% (range 7.5–84.7%) were CD8+ (Table 1). Other cell types present included CD19+ B cells (median 2.5%, range 0–10.7%) and CD56/CD16+ NK cells (median 0.9%, range 0.2–1.6%). Intracellular cytokine analysis following recall with the custom pool of peptides was used to assess SARS‐CoV‐2 specificity, followed by intracellular cytokine analysis to define reactivity to each peptide epitope. All batches of VST included antigen‐specific CD4+ T cells (Figure 1a) and CD8+ T cells (Figure 1b) and recognised multiple epitopes restricted by multiple HLA class I and II alleles (Table 1). Batches of VST were also assessed for alloreactivity against a panel of HLA‐transfected K562 cells. Alloreactive responses were not detectable in any of the six batches (Supplementary figure 1).

sec.title: Participant characteristics and treatment
sec.p: Between September 2022 and June 2023, six participants with high‐risk SARS‐CoV‐2 infection and/or end organ disease were enrolled in the study. A clinical profile of each participant is provided in Table 2. All participants had prior SARS‐CoV‐2 vaccination, were B‐cell‐deficient at the time of recruitment and had received prior SARS‐CoV‐2‐directed therapies. They had been diagnosed with SARS‐CoV‐2 infection between 7 and 73 days prior to the commencement of T‐cell therapy. All participants received their first VST infusion within 4 days of enrolment. The batch of VST provided to each participant was selected based on a minimum of one matched HLA allele displaying SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific restriction (Table 3). Participants received up to two fixed doses of 4 × 107 cells at a 2‐week interval and were assessed for safety, virological/clinical disease resolution and SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell immunity at 2, 4 and 12 weeks after the first dose. A summary of the clinical outcome of each participant is provided in Table 3. Two participants did not complete follow‐up. The first participant (QRCOV1‐01) died 20 days after the commencement of T‐cell therapy, and the sixth participant (QRCOV01‐06) received only a single infusion because of a grade 4 serious adverse event (SAE).

sec.title: Safety profile of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy
sec.p: Recruitment was terminated after the treatment of six participants because of infrequent incidence of symptomatic COVID‐19 infection in the Australian population. The primary endpoint of the study was safety, with adverse events graded per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5. Allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy was well tolerated in five of the six participants, with only one grade 2 event deemed unlikely to be because of T‐cell infusion (Table 4). This event was attributed to the progression of pulmonary parenchymal damage sustained earlier in the course of COVID‐19. This participant received SARS‐CoV‐2 T‐cell therapy 73 days after initial infection. Participant QRCOV01‐06 experienced a grade 4 SAE associated with respiratory failure following a single VST infusion. One day after T‐cell infusion, the participant developed cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and multiple episodes of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage confirmed on bronchoscopy, requiring intubation and intensive care support. The participant was subsequently treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, high‐dose corticosteroids, etanercept and azithromycin. The patient ultimately recovered and was discharged from hospital. This participant had an underlying inflammatory autoimmune disease.

sec.title: Virological and clinical monitoring following SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy
sec.p: The five participants who received two doses of VST were monitored for changes in SARS‐CoV‐2 viral load using a nasopharyngeal swab (NPS) immediately prior to the first and second infusions, and at 4 weeks after the commencement of VST. A standard curve generated using synthetic SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA control was used to determine viral copies (Figure 2). Ongoing hospital‐based monitoring of viral load using NPS was also performed at the discretion of the treating clinician (Supplementary table 5). Relevant anatomical imaging was used to assess changes in pulmonary parenchyma and COVID‐19 lung disease. These five participants demonstrated a reduction in viral load following VST therapy (Figure 2). QRCOV1‐01, who had previously received multiple rounds of anti‐viral treatment because of severe COVID‐19 associated with bilateral ground glass changes and focal airspace opacification in the left lingual, demonstrated a reduction in viral load 12 days after commencement of VST (Figure 2a). Despite initial clinical improvement, the participant experienced further deterioration with febrile neutropenia and proven Enterobacter cloacae urosepsis. In this setting of evolving pulmonary fibrosis, the participant died 20 days after the commencement of VST. QRCOV1‐02 (Figure 2b) and QRCOV1‐03 (Figure 2c) both had a single line of anti‐viral treatment prior to recruitment to the study. Both participants demonstrated a decline in NPS viral load following VST, and by 4 weeks, they had no detectable viral load and stable respiratory function. Following successful resolution of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, QRCOV1‐02 progressed to a scheduled allogeneic HSCT. QRCOV1‐04 (Figure 2d) and QRCOV1‐05 (Figure 2e) had multiple lines of anti‐viral treatment prior to their recruitment into the study. Both participants displayed patchy infiltrates and opacification in the lung prior to the commencement of VST. Following VST, QRCOV1‐04 and QRCOV1‐05 demonstrated a reduction in NPS viral load and reduced opacification of the lungs. However, they both remained SARS‐CoV‐2 positive throughout the course of the study (Supplementary table 5). QRCOV1‐05 was readmitted to hospital 64 days after commencement of VST with ongoing breathlessness and fever and received further anti‐viral treatment (Figure 2e). A subsequent chest CT scan on Day 65 revealed further improvement in lung function.

sec.title: Immune monitoring following SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy
sec.p: To investigate changes in immunity following VST, we initially looked for changes in the frequency of blood immune cell subsets. All participants remained B‐cell‐deficient throughout the course of the study; however, we observed no consistent changes in the blood profile of other immune cell subsets following VST (Supplementary figure 2). To assess changes in the SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell response following VST, we employed a whole blood cytokine release assay. Following overnight stimulation with either the spike antigen or other SARS‐CoV‐2 (non‐spike) antigens, we assessed both IFN‐γ and IL‐2 production using a cytometric bead array. As a control, we compared the magnitude of these responses to a cohort of healthy controls who had resolved SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. As we had previously observed, IL‐2 was more sensitive for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell immunity in whole blood. Most of the participants displayed a low spike‐specific IL‐2 response (Figure 3a) and non‐spike‐specific IL‐2 response (Figure 3b) prior to VST. Four of five participants demonstrated an increase in spike‐specific and non‐spike‐specific IL‐2 following the first VST infusion. Similar responses were observed for IFN‐γ, with an increased response to spike (Figure 3c) and non‐spike antigens (Figure 3d) in three of five participants. QRCOV1‐05 demonstrated an initial decline in response to spike and non‐spike antigens following VST, while QRCOV1‐01 demonstrated a decline in the IFN‐γ response to spike and non‐spike antigens.

sec.p: To assess other changes in the peripheral immune profile that could be associated with both viral control and an increase in the SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell response, we performed a 96‐parameter cytokine/chemokine array on plasma samples from participants taken throughout the course of the study. While the majority of cytokines and chemokines did not show any discernible trends following VST (Supplementary table 6), we observed a consistent increase in the concentration of IL‐12p40 in the plasma of participants 2 weeks after their initial dose (Figure 3e). IL‐12p40 concentration continued to increase in three of four participants who were assessed at the 4‐week time point and then declined in all participants by the 12‐week time point.

sec.title: Changes in the T‐cell repertoire following SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy
sec.p: We have previously shown in solid organ transplant recipients that viral control following VST therapy is associated with changes in the T‐cell repertoire in the periphery. 9 To determine whether we could see a similar pattern in the HSCT recipients receiving SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy, we employed T‐cell receptor beta variable (TRBV) complementarity‐determining region 3 (CDR3) deep sequencing on PBMC samples from the four participants who completed the follow‐up. To assess whether we could detect T cells from the product in patients following VST, we compared PBMC TRBV sequences to the T‐cell product TRBV sequences. To limit our analysis to the memory T‐cell compartment, we only included CDR3 sequences with n ≥ 2. In the four participants assessed, we detected no T‐cell product‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences in QRCOV1‐02 (Figure 4a), one at Day 28 in patient QRCOV1‐03 (Figure 4b), and none in QRCOV1‐04 (Figure 4c) and QRCOV1‐05 (Figure 4d). However, we saw the apparent emergence of new CDR3 sequences following VST in all four participants; some were maintained for the duration of the study.

sec.p: One limitation of our observations on the T‐cell landscape was the variability in the depth of sequencing in the patient samples (Supplementary table 7). We therefore next sought to identify SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences in our participants using a more stringent cut‐off. We analysed our samples using ImmunoSEQ T‐MAP COVID, a database of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences identified in previous studies. We also limited our data to sequences with > 2 templates and a productive frequency greater than the minimum productive frequency prior to the first infusion (Day 0). From this analysis, we identified potential SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences in all participants (Supplementary table 8). This included sequences present prior to therapy in QRCOV1‐02 (n = 39; Figure 5a), QRCOV1‐03 (n = 23; Figure 5b), QRCOV1‐04 (n = 29; Figure 5c) and QRCOV1‐05 (n = 53; Figure 5d). The majority of these sequences either remained stable or declined after VST, excluding a single sequence in QRCOV1‐05 with 100‐fold expansion between Days 0 and 84. We also detected other potential SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences that were only evident following therapy in QRCOV1‐02 (n = 30; Figure 5e), QRCOV1‐03 (n = 126; Figure 5f), QRCOV1‐04 (n = 43; Figure 5g) and QRCOV1‐05 (n = 87; Figure 5h). In QRCOV1‐02 (n = 203), we also observed the emergence of a novel set of potential SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences following HSCT, which were likely donor‐derived. The immunoSEQ T‐MAP COVID provides the identity of peptide epitopes recognised by the SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences. We collated the number of different epitopes recognised by each participant and compared the number before and after VST. All participants showed an increase in the number of predicted epitopes after VST (Figure 6). The observation of new SARS‐COV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 sequences and an increase in the number of epitope targets suggest that treatment with SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy may promote the broadening of the T‐cell response via epitope spread.

sec.title: Immune profiling in participant QRCOV1‐06
sec.p: Although we had limited material available from participant QRCOV1‐06 because of the rapid onset of CRS and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage following the first dose of VST, we performed some follow‐up analysis to investigate any potential association between the VST product or underlying immunity in the participant and potential aetiology for the SAE. Batch THI‐COV‐003 was not used in any other participants during the study; however, we observed no discernible differences in the cell phenotype between THI‐COV‐003 and the other batches used in the study (Table 1, Supplementary table 4). THI‐COV‐003 displayed no alloreactivity when assessed following manufacture (Supplementary figure 1), and a follow‐up alloreactivity assessment between the THI‐COV‐003 VST, a panel of EBV‐transformed B cells encoding participant HLA and participant PBMC, revealed no alloreactivity (Supplementary figure 3). This suggested that a direct alloreactive response was unlikely to be the cause of the SAE. We were also able to assess the SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell immunity at baseline in this participant, prior to VST. In contrast to the other participants enrolled in the study, whose T cells displayed no or low interferon gamma (IFN‐γ) production in response to both non‐spike and spike antigen prior to VST, QRCOV1‐06 had a strong IFN‐γ response to the non‐spike antigens (Figure 7a). The participant also showed an elevated interleukin 2 (IL‐2) response to spike, comparable to that observed in QRCOV1‐05 (Figure 7b). Finally, we assessed the cytokine/chemokine in the plasma of QRCOV1‐06 before treatment, noting that we were not able to obtain additional samples during the SAE. Most cytokine/chemokine concentrations overlapped with the levels found in the five other participants prior to VST (Supplementary figure 4). However, we observed a higher concentration of IL‐31 in the plasma of QRCOV1‐06 (Figure 7c).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Adoptive transfer of VST has been clinically employed to reduce morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients with a range of viral infections. 4 , 10 , 11 The continuing emergence of novel viral strains and the varied responsiveness of immunocompromised individuals to vaccines and anti‐viral drugs highlight the ongoing need for alternate approaches, including targeted cellular therapies, to treat at‐risk patients. A number of recent studies have demonstrated the strong safety profile and potential efficacy of using SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T cells to treat COVID‐19. 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 In the current study, we demonstrate the feasibility of our SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific allogeneic T‐cell bank; however, we highlight some differences in the safety profile, where one participant with a discrepant baseline SARS‐CoV‐2 IFN‐γ response to non‐spike antigens experienced an SAE, suggesting that underlying viral immunity could contribute to rapid severe complications following VST therapy.

The critical contribution of T‐cell immunity during primary SARS‐CoV‐2 infection is well established. 16 , 17 , 18 T‐cell immunity also plays an important role in the control of SARS‐CoV‐2 breakthrough infection following vaccination. 19 , 20 Immunocompromised individuals, including cancer patients, are known to be at increased risk of severe COVID‐19. 21 Multiple studies have demonstrated that immunocompromised cohorts, including patients with solid cancer, haematological cancer or immune‐mediated inflammatory disorders, display delayed seroconversion in response to COVID‐19 vaccination in comparison with immunocompetent individuals. 22 , 23 , 24 These findings are consistent with the observations made in transplant recipient cohorts. 25 , 26 In addition, a therapeutic pre‐conditioning component of HSCT involves profound and prolonged immune suppression, which leaves patients at high risk of infection‐derived complications. 22 Standard‐of‐care, evidence‐based clinical interventions for symptomatic COVID‐19 in patients with immunodeficiency have included dexamethasone and remdesivir to treat moderate‐to‐severe illness, and/or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir depending on clinical severity and pharmacokinetic interaction. 27 , 28 , 29 Monupiravir can be used to treat outpatients with mild/moderate COVID‐19. 30 , 31 Prophylactic interventions, such as tixagevimab/cilgavimab, have been administered to immunocompromised, at‐risk individuals and are well tolerated by haematology patients. 32

Severe COVID‐19 can lead to pulmonary parenchymal abnormalities even in patients without pre‐existing lung disease. 33 , 34 More than 5% of SARS‐CoV‐2‐infected patients develop pneumonia followed by acute respiratory distress syndrome and require mechanical ventilation. 35 In the current study, three participants underwent high‐resolution chest scans to monitor pulmonary pathology, two of whom demonstrated resolution of ground glass opacification following the administration of VST (participants QRCOV‐04 and QRCOV‐05). While the other participant, QRCOV‐01, demonstrated initial improvement in lung function and was removed from oxygen support following VST, they succumbed to progressive pulmonary fibrosis, radiological evidence of which was present prior to VST. This participant was recruited to the trial 70+ days after initial diagnosis of infection, emphasising the need for early interventions to reduce the development of long‐term pulmonary complications.

SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy was well tolerated by five of six recipients. QRCOV1‐06 received only a single dose of VST after developing clinical CRS following the first infusion. This participant had a history of kidney transplant and underlying lupus nephritis. Alveolar haemorrhage is a known rare complication in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). 36 , 37 Previous observations have demonstrated an interaction between SLE and COVID‐19, which included an exacerbated inflammatory response. 38 Case studies have also reported alveolar haemorrhaging in SLE patients with COVID‐19. 39 It is therefore likely that this participant had an increased underlying risk of alveolar haemorrhage. This participant was also unique in the patient cohort because of the presence of a strong SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell response prior to VST that may also have contributed to the pulmonary complications following VST. Previous observations have also indicated that on rare occasions, on‐target toxicity can lead to SAEs. In an early study from our group, a patient death following VST therapy for Epstein–Barr virus‐associated post‐transplant lymphoproliferative disease was associated with the lysis of EBV‐infected tumor cells in the wall of a vein in direct communication with the bronchus. 40 VST therapy has also been associated with possible on‐target toxicity in other studies. 41 Further studies are required to determine whether this was an isolated incident or whether participants with similar underlying disease phenotypes are at a similar risk following the administration of VST.

TRBV TCR deep sequencing is a widely employed strategy to study the impact and longevity of adoptively transferred VST. Recent observations in patients treated with CAR‐T‐cell therapy have demonstrated the survival of immunodominant T‐cell clonotypes for more than a decade following complete clinical remission. 42 Studies using VST have demonstrated that transferred T cells can survive for more than a decade following transfer. 43 We have also previously demonstrated that changes in the peripheral T‐cell repertoire in transplant patients following VST therapy are observed with recovery from viral disease. 9 Since the emergence of COVID‐19, a multitude of studies have defined the SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell repertoire that provides a large repository of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell receptors. 7 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 We saw limited evidence of allogeneic TRBV TCR sequences in circulation following VST. This is consistent with other studies in which allogeneic VST has been rarely found in the circulation of recipients. In a similar study using SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific VST, Vasileiou et al. 13 reported the detection of VST‐derived TCR following infusion; however, the frequency of their TCR is not provided. In the present study, we saw changes in the global TRBV landscape that were associated with a reduction in viral load following VST therapy. These changes were associated with the emergence of novel SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV sequences that were not present prior to administration. This was consistent with the increased SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific cytokine production following VST therapy and is evidence of the longer‐term establishment of functional SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell memory.

Although difficult to identify, previous studies have suggested that VST therapy can induce epitope spreading, most likely through the release of antigen from virus‐infected cells. 48 , 49 In a previous study of solid organ transplant patients treated with autologous cytomegalovirus (CMV)‐specific VST, we observed the emergence of novel TRBV sequences following therapy. 9 Neuenhahn et al. 50 demonstrated using minimally manipulated CMV‐specific VST therapy that CMV‐specific immune reconstitution was associated with the emergence of endogenous T‐cell responses rather than the expansion of the allogeneic VST. Prockop et al. 51 showed that while allogeneic CMV‐specific VST could be detected up to 56 days following therapy in HSCT patients, long‐term immune responses were generated by HSCT donor or host CMV‐specific T cells.

The results of the current study support previous findings that the administration of allogeneic off‐the‐shelf SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapy to HLA‐matched participants with an immunocompromised status is generally safe 12 ; however, further study is required to determine whether the SAE we observed in one participant is associated with an underlying disease phenotype. Our results also provide further evidence for epitope spread as a mechanism through which allogeneic VST promote long‐term reconstitution of virus‐specific T‐cell immunity.

sec.title: Ethical approvals
sec.p: To generate a bank of allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell therapies, healthy blood donors were recruited from a pre‐existing convalescent SARS‐CoV‐2 cohort. 45 Approval for the cell therapy manufacturing project and clinical trial (ACTRN12622000377730) was obtained from the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute Human Research Ethics Committee. A total of 46 healthy control participants who had recovered from SARS‐CoV‐2 infection were included as part of the comparative analysis in the study. Ethics approval for the recruitment of these participants was provided by the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute Human Research Ethics Committee. All participants in the projects described above provided written informed consent prior to undertaking any study‐specific activities.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: We conducted an investigator‐initiated, open‐label, uncontrolled phase I clinical trial (ACTRN12622000377730) for patients who were SARS‐CoV‐2 positive and at risk of severe COVID‐19 because of immunosuppressive therapy, transplantation or chemotherapy/malignancy. Participants were recruited from a single site, The Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital, which is a tertiary referral centre for haematology and stem cell transplantation. The inclusion criteria included age 18 years or above; active SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, confirmed by rapid antigen test or polymerase chain reaction; immunosuppression because of transplantation, receipt of immunosuppressive therapy or receipt of chemotherapy to treat malignancy; and availability of a suitable batch of VST therapy. Exclusion criteria included a psychiatric condition that may compromise the ability to participate in this trial; women who are pregnant, lactating or women of child‐bearing potential who are unwilling to use adequate contraception; any other medical condition that would prohibit participation; and active acute graft‐versus‐host disease (GvHD) grade ≥ 2 or chronic GvHD requiring ≥ 0.5 mg kg−1 prednisolone. Participants were either of known HLA type or had HLA typing performed to enable choice of the appropriate VST batch. Participants were able to receive all other standard‐of‐care therapies, and recruitment was not stratified for underlying disease or treatment conferring risk of severe COVID‐19, or prior therapies, including prophylactic monoclonal antibodies or COVID vaccination or therapy for COVID‐19 prior to study entry. Unless otherwise stated, participants received two infusions of 4 × 107 cells 2 weeks apart. Participants were monitored for a period of 12 weeks following the first infusion. The primary endpoint was the safety of adoptive immunotherapy using allogeneic SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T cells, measured by CTCAE version 5. The secondary endpoint was the kinetics of virus‐specific immunity following treatment, and exploratory endpoints included the effect on SARS‐CoV‐2 viral load and clinical response to treatment. The study was initially designed to recruit 20 participants; however, because of increased vaccine coverage in Australia and less clinically severe COVID‐19, the trial was closed following the recruitment of six participants.

sec.title: VST therapy manufacturing and characterisation
sec.p: Clinical‐grade allogeneic T‐cell products were manufactured from PBMC derived from healthy donors who had recovered from prior SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, in accordance with published protocols. 7 Donors were selected to provide broad HLA coverage across common HLA alleles in the Australian population (Supplementary table 1). The SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific (THI‐COV) T‐cell products were generated using two custom‐designed peptide pools containing SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific CD4+ and CD8+ T‐cell epitopes (Supplementary tables 2 and 3). HLA restriction of each epitope was defined using a standard HLA‐restriction assay. For VST manufacture, PBMC were isolated from healthy donor blood then cryopreserved prior to VST manufacture. Subsequently, PBMC were thawed and stimulated with the peptide pools (Mimotopes, Mulgrave, VIC, Australia) and cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 5% human AB serum and recombinant interleukin 2 (IL‐2; 120 IU mL−1; catalogue no. 170‐076‐14; Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) for 14–17 days. T‐cell products were cryopreserved in Albumex 4 (catalogue no. 34500165; CSL Behring, Melbourne, VIC, Australia) containing 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (catalogue no. WAK‐DMSO‐10; WAK‐Chemie Medical, Steinbach, Germany). Antigen specificity of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific T‐cell batches was determined using an intracellular cytokine assay. T‐cell release criteria included > 70% viability post‐thaw, > 70% CD3+ T cells post‐thaw, negative for microbial growth, negative for mycoplasma and < 3 EU mL−1 endotoxin.

sec.title: Intracellular cytokine assays
sec.p: Intracellular cytokine assays were used to define the specificity and HLA restriction of VST generated for adoptive T‐cell therapy, in a two‐step process. To demonstrate SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific reactivity, VST products were recalled with the custom‐designed peptide pools containing SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific CD4+ and CD8+ T‐cell epitopes. CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells were then assessed for the expression of IFN‐γ, tumor necrosis factor, IL‐2, and/or CD107a. Antibodies used in the study are provided in Supplementary table 9. Products were then assessed for reactivity to individual HLA‐matched peptide epitopes using an IFN‐γ intracellular cytokine assay. Epitopes were selected for testing based on a confirmed HLA restriction that matched the HLA type of the VST product. Flow cytometric acquisition was performed using a BD LSR Fortessa cell analyser with FACSDiva software (BD Biosciences, Melbourne, VIC, Australia). T‐cell reactivity to a virus‐specific peptide pool or HLA‐restricted peptide epitope was considered positive if the response was greater than the mean plus three standard deviations of the response of VST cultured in the absence of stimulus. Post‐acquisition analysis was also performed using FlowJo software (FlowJo, Ashland, OR, USA). The gating strategy used to define virus‐specific T‐cell reactivity is provided in Supplementary figure 5.

sec.title: Assessment of T‐cell alloreactivity
sec.p: Potential alloreactivity of VST manufactured for allogeneic use was assessed using a panel of K562 cell lines, each transfected with a single HLA class I allele. VST products were incubated with each K562‐HLA class I cell line at a responder‐to‐stimulator ratio of 10:1 and assessed for intracellular IFN‐γ production. Products were considered alloreactive against an HLA class I allele if > 1% of lymphocytes produced IFN‐γ following subtraction of the background response generated against untransfected K562 cells. 52

sec.title: PCR detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 viral load
sec.p: Nasopharyngeal swabs were collected and transported in Copan eNat solution (catalogue no. 606C; Interpath, Somerton, VIC, Australia) prior to the first and second infusion and at 4 weeks following the commencement of VST therapy. RNA was extracted from this solution using the MagMax viral RNA extraction kit (catalogue no. AM1939; Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). RT‐PCR was performed with primers and probes targeting the SARS‐CoV‐2 N1 gene (catalogue nos 10006821, 100006822 and 10006823; IDT, Coralville, IA, USA) compared to a standard curve using 1 in 10 dilutions of Twist synthetic SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA control (catalogue no. TWB102019; Decode Science, Mt Waverley, VIC, Australia). RNAseP primers and probes were also used for a positive control of each sample (catalogue nos 10006827, 10006828 and 10006829; IDT). RT‐PCR was run and analysed on the Bio‐Rad CFX 96 well machine.

sec.title: Whole blood cytokine assay
sec.p: The whole blood assay used to assess SARS‐Cov‐2‐specific T‐cell responses has been previously described. 45 Heparinised whole blood was incubated with overlapping peptide pools of SARS‐CoV‐2 proteins including ORF3A, ORF6, ORF7A, ORF7B, ORF8, ORF9, ORF10, nucleocapsid, membrane protein, envelope protein and spike glycoprotein (JPT Technologies, Berlin, Germany). The plate was incubated overnight at 37°C in a CO2 incubator; then, plasma supernatant was collected and stored at −80°C. IFN‐γ and IL‐2 cytokine analysis was performed using a cytometric bead array (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) as previously described. 45 Samples were acquired using a BD LSRFortessa with FACSDiva software (BD Biosciences), and post‐acquisition cytokine analysis was performed using FCAP array software (BD Biosciences). The cytokine response to each peptide pool was calculated following subtraction of the spontaneous cytokine released from blood incubated without peptide.

sec.title: Whole blood cell phenotyping
sec.p: Whole Blood (50 μL) samples were transferred to a BD Trucount Tube (BD Biosciences) and incubated with anti CCR7 PE‐Cy7. After 10 min, the following antibodies were added: CD45RA FITC, CD38 PerCP‐Cy5.5, CD45 APC, CD4 RF718, Live/Dead NIR, CD56 BV421, CD28 BV480, CD3 BV711, CD8 Super Bright 780, CD16 PE, CD27 PE‐Dazzle 594 and CD19 PE‐Cy5. Antibodies used for cell phenotyping are provided in Supplementary table 9. Samples were then incubated with BD FACS™ Lysing Solution for 15 min. Samples were acquired using a BD LSRFortessa with FACSDiva software. Post‐acquisition analysis was also performed using FlowJo software. The gating strategy used to define cell populations is provided in Supplementary figure 6.

sec.title: Genomic DNA T‐cell receptor sequencing
sec.p: Peripheral blood was collected from participants prior to the first VST infusion and 2, 4 and 12 weeks after the first infusion. PBMC were then isolated from blood, and DNA was extracted from 5 × 106 PBMC per sample. DNA was also extracted from the six VST products generated for the study. TRBV deep sequencing was then performed by ImmunoSEQ® (Adaptive Biotechnologies, Seattle, WA, USA). The TRBV CDR3 dataset was then extracted from the Adaptive Biotechnologies ImmunoSEQ Analyzer, out‐of‐frame and stop sequences were excluded from analysis, and a template cut‐off > 2 was selected. The CDR3 sequence for each template was combined with the corresponding V gene and J gene to create a variable CDR3_V_J. Venn diagram, which were then used to analyse the overlap between participant samples from each time point and the corresponding product used for VST. An exact CDR3_V_J match was required in order to identify the sequences as overlapping.

sec.title: Identification of potential SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3
sec.p: To identify the presence of SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV sequences within the PBMC of participants, we used the COVID Search Tool in the ImmunoSEQ Analyzer. Supplementary table 8 provides a summary of the potential SARS‐CoV‐2‐specific TRBV CDR3 identified at each time point for the four participants in the study who completed follow‐up analysis. The table also includes the antigen (reference_orfs) and peptide (reference_amino_acids) recognised by the TRBV CDR3. To minimise the impact of lower total templates in samples prior to the first infusion, we used a cut‐off of greater than the minimum productive frequency prior to the first infusion (Day 0). The data were then curated to separate TRBV sequences present prior to the commencement of VST and those that were only detectable following VST. The frequency of these TRBV sequences at each time point were then plotted using Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).
